# Volume 2 — XXV An Brierley Scandal

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

On a cheerful June morning, two weeks following the storm of Uncle Zeb, Nell emerged lazily from the garden into the Grey Shutters yard, holding a pair of withered white narcissus stems in her hands.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0000 }

“Look, Thirza,” she uttered mournfully, raising the blossoms in front of the gaze of a stern woman, whose hair was covered by a green gingham apron, as she made her way indoors carrying a featherless chicken, “these represent the sole buds unharmed by the tempest . . . and even those are damaged. I’m so sorry . . . I wished for a few for Obed’s grave. He was forever so fond of June lilies.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0001 }

“To tell the truth, I miss them too,” Thirza conceded, “even if grieving for them feels wrong after such greater disasters. . . the destruction of all the crops in addition to the fruit.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0002 }

“However, folks have re-sown their oats,” Nell remarked reassuringly, “and Mr. Pettifer mentions that in his opinion provided there is a favorable summer they will turn out fine albeit belatedly. Moreover, my annuals are all sprouting anew . . . yet alas, no substitute exists for the June lilies. Unfortunate little Dinah Wren will be without any as well. I traveled the entire distance back to her garden yesterday evening, yet not a single one remained. I feel certain she will feel their loss.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0003 }

“I truly do not believe you should make those kinds of statements, Nell,” Thirza remarked sternly. “Thirty years have passed since Dinah Wren died, and her soul resides in heaven . . . at least, I trust it does.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0004 }

“Yes, but my belief is that she remains fond of and still recalls her garden in this place,” Nell stated. “I am certain that regardless of my length of stay in heaven, I would want to gaze below and observe a person placing blossoms upon my burial site. Had a garden such as Dinah Wren’s belonged to me here, a period exceeding thirty years, even within heaven, would be required before I ceased feeling longings for home at times.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0005 }

“Well, do not allow the twins to listen to you speaking in that manner,” Thirza protested weakly, carrying her chicken inside the house as she did so.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0006 }

Attaching her narcissi to her hair, Nell proceeded to the lane gate, where she remained briefly basking in the June radiance prior to heading inside to take care of her chores for Saturday morning. Beauty was returning to the world; ancient Mother Nature was exerting every effort to erase the storm's marks, and even if full success would elude her for numerous moons, she was truly performing miracles.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0007 }

“It would be wonderful if I could simply do nothing for the rest of the day,” Nell remarked to a bluebird that was warbling and swaying upon a willow branch, “however, a schoolma’am who likewise assists in raising twins is forbidden from giving in to idleness, birdie. Your song is so lovely, little bird. You are expressing the emotions in my soul through your music far superior to anything I could manage on my own. Oh, who is approaching?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0008 }

A delivery cart came rattling along the path, carrying a pair of passengers in the front and a large chest in the rear. As the vehicle approached, Nell identified the man driving as the child of the station master at Alder River; however, the person beside him was unfamiliar . . . a tiny female who leapt agilely to the ground by the entrance even before the horse fully stopped. This individual was a most attractive small lady, clearly closer to fifty than forty years of age, yet possessing blushing cheeks, gleaming dark eyes, and glossy dark locks, topped with a remarkable hat adorned with flowers and feathers. Although she had traveled eight miles along a dirty highway, her appearance was as immaculate as though she had newly emerged from the well-known bandbox.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0009 }

“Does Mr. James A. Pettifer reside in this place?” she asked in a prompt manner.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0010 }

“No, Mr. Pettifer resides in that direction,” said Nell, entirely consumed by surprise.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0011 }

“Indeed, it struck me that this residence appeared excessively neat . . . far too neat for James A. to be residing in, provided he has not altered significantly since the time I was acquainted with him,” trilled the small woman. “Is it accurate that James A. intends to wed a certain woman who resides within this village?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0012 }

“Oh no, no,” Nell exclaimed, her face turning red with such an expression of guilt that the unfamiliar woman gazed at her inquisitively, almost as though she harbored a suspicion that Nell entertained plans to marry Mr. Pettifer.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0013 }

“Yet I read it within an Island newspaper,” maintained the Fair Unknown. “I received a marked edition from a friend . . . acquaintances show such constant eagerness for those actions. Over ‘new citizen,’ James A.‘s name had been inscribed.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0014 }

“Oh, that letter was just supposed to be a gag,” Nell panted. “Mr. Pettifer does not plan to take anyone as a wife. I promise you he doesn’t.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0015 }

“Hearing that gives me great joy,” stated the woman with the rosy complexion, as she agilely ascended to her place in the wagon once more, “for it so occurs that he is currently wed. His spouse is me. Ah, you have good reason to appear astonished. It seems to me he has been posing as an unmarried man while shattering hearts everywhere. Oh dear, James A.,” she said, bobbing her head forcefully across the countryside toward the lengthy white dwelling, “the time for your amusement has passed. Here I am . . . yet I would not have troubled myself to arrive had I not suspected you were engaging in some wrongdoing. Is that bird of his,” she inquired, facing Nell, “still as full of foul language as before?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0016 }

“His parrot . . . has died . . . it seems to me,” breathed unfortunate Nell, for whom even her own name was uncertain at that exact second.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0017 }

“Deceased! That means everything will turn out fine,” the rosy lady exclaimed with joy. “With that bird gone, James A. will be easy for me to handle.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0018 }

After making that enigmatic statement, she proceeded happily on her path, prompting Nell to rush over to the kitchen entrance in order to greet Thirza.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0019 }

“Nell, who was that woman?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0020 }

“Thirza,” Nell said, her eyes sparkling even as her manner remained serious, “is there anything about my appearance that suggests insanity?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0021 }

“No extra amount than normally,” Thirza uttered, intending no sarcasm whatsoever.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0022 }

“Well then, do you suppose that I am awake?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0023 }

“Nell, what absurd idea has taken hold of you? I demand to know, who was that woman?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0024 }

“Thirza, unless I have lost my mind or am dreaming, it is impossible for her to be the mere material of dreams . . . she has to be actual. Regardless, I am certain a bonnet like that is beyond my imagination. She claims to be the wife of Mr. Pettifer, Thirza.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0025 }

Thirza likewise directed her gaze back.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0026 }

“His spouse! Nell Harcourt! Why, then, has he been pretending to be single?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0027 }

“I really don’t imagine he did,” Nell remarked, attempting to remain fair. “He didn’t ever state that he was unmarried. Everyone just assumed it. Oh Thirza, how is Mrs. Sowerby going to react to this?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0028 }

They discovered the news from Mrs. Sowerby upon her arrival later that night. Mrs. Sowerby experienced no astonishment whatsoever! Mrs. Sowerby had perpetually anticipated an event of this nature! Mrs. Sowerby had constantly recognized that Mr. Pettifer possessed a peculiar quality!
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0029 }

“To imagine him abandoning his wife!” she exclaimed with indignation. “It resembles a story you would come across in the States, yet who would anticipate something like this occurring right here in Brierley?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0030 }

“However, we are not certain that she was abandoned by him,” Nell objected, resolute in considering her friend guiltless until guilt had been demonstrated. “We are entirely ignorant of the truth behind the matter.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0031 }

“Indeed, it won't be long before we do. I intend to head right across to that place,” declared Mrs. Sowerby, a woman who was entirely ignorant of the concept of delicacy. “Officially, her coming is unknown to me, but Mr. Pettifer was scheduled to fetch a prescription for Thomas from Delford this afternoon, which provides a suitable pretext. Once I uncover every detail, I will stop by to inform you as I return.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0032 }

Mrs. Sowerby hurried into the situation that Nell was too afraid to enter. No persuasion could have forced Nell to cross over to the Pettifer residence; nonetheless, possessing her fair and rightful portion of inquisitiveness, she was privately pleased that Mrs. Sowerby intended to unravel the secret. She and Thirza eagerly anticipated the return of that worthy woman, yet their waiting proved useless. Mrs. Sowerby failed to return to Grey Shutters that evening. Upon coming home at nine o’clock from the Gammon place, Robin provided the reason.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0033 }

“I ran into Mrs. Sowerby along with a woman I didn’t know in the Hollow,” he stated, “and goodness, the two of them were chatting simultaneously! Mrs. Sowerby asked me to pass along her apologies that it was too late to visit this evening. Nell, I’m terribly hungry. Milty’s was where we took tea at four o’clock, and I feel Mrs. Gammon is truly stingy. She provided us with no preserves or cake . . . and there was barely any bread, either.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0034 }

“Robin, whenever you pay a visit, you ought not to ever find fault with any food offered to you,” Nell remarked with gravity. “Such behavior shows extremely poor etiquette.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0035 }

“Very well . . . I will merely think it,” Robin stated happily. “Nell, please grant a guy some dinner.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0036 }

Nell turned her gaze toward Thirza, who came behind her into the pantry and carefully closed the door.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0037 }

“You may spread a bit of jam upon his bread, for I am aware of the usual nature of tea at Levi Gammon’s.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0038 }

With a sigh, Robin accepted his piece of bread and jam.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0039 }

“When all is said and done, it’s a rather disappointing world,” he observed. “Milty owns a cat that suffers from fits . . . every single day for three weeks, she’s had a fit. Milty claims watching her is tremendous fun. I made a trip down today specifically to catch her having a fit, yet the miserable old thing refused to suffer one and simply remained completely healthy, even though Milty and I lingered about the entire afternoon and waited. But it doesn't matter” . . . Robin cheered up as the subtle solace of the plum jam seeped into his spirit . . . “perhaps I'll still get to see her in one sometime. Since she’s been so accustomed to it, it doesn’t seem probable that she’d cease having them all of a sudden, does it? This jam is extremely delicious.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0040 }

Robin was free of any griefs that plum jam was unable to heal.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0041 }

Because Sunday turned out to be exceedingly wet, no one could venture outside; nevertheless, all persons had learned a variation of the Pettifer account by Monday. The school hummed with the news, and Robin returned to the house, packed with details.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0042 }

“Thirza, Mr. Pettifer possesses a different wife . . . well, not precisely different, yet according to Milty they have ceased being wed for a considerable duration. My assumption was always that folks were required to remain wedded once they started, but Milty claims otherwise, stating methods exist to cease if agreement is impossible. Milty states a single method involves simply departing from your wife, which is the action Mr. Pettifer took. Milty claims Mr. Pettifer departed from his wife owing to her hurling items toward him . . . solid items . . . whereas Arty Mott claims the reason was her refusal to permit his smoking, and Ned Clay claims the reason was her constant scolding toward him. My own wife would not be left by ME over such matters. My choice would be simply planting my foot and stating, ‘Mrs. Robin, you’ve just got to do what’ll please me ’cause I’m a man.’ My guess is that would resolve her rather fast. Conversely, Annetta Clay claims the departure was hers on account of his refusal to clean his boots by the entrance, and she holds no fault against her. I am heading straight across to Mr. Pettifer’s at this very moment to observe her nature.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0043 }

Before long, Robin came back, looking a bit dispirited.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0044 }

“Mrs. Pettifer was absent . . . she has traveled to Delford alongside Mrs. Agatha Sowerby in order to purchase fresh wallpaper for the parlor. Also, Mr. Pettifer instructed that Nell be told to visit him over there since he desires to speak with her. Furthermore, the floor has been scrubbed, and Mr. Pettifer has shaved, even though no preaching took place yesterday.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0045 }

To Nell, the appearance of the Pettifer kitchen seemed extremely unusual. Indeed, the floor had been washed to a remarkable degree of cleanliness, as had every piece of furniture present; the stove was shined to such an extent that it reflected her face; the walls had been given a coat of whitewash, and the window glass glistened under the sun. Beside the table, Mr. Pettifer was seated in his work garments, which had possessed various rips and tears on Friday, yet were currently tidily mended and swept. He had been cleanly shaven, and the small amount of hair remaining on his head had been attentively cut.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0046 }

“Take a seat, Nell, take a seat,” Mr. Pettifer urged, speaking in a voice almost identical to the one residents of Brierley employed during funeral services. “Emily has headed to Delford alongside Agatha Sowerby . . . already, she has formed an enduring bond of friendship with Agatha Sowerby. The sheer perversity of women surpasses everything. Ah, Nell, my days of comfort have come to an end . . . completely ended. I imagine it will be order and cleanliness for me throughout my remaining days.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0047 }

Although Mr. Pettifer attempted to sound sorrowful, he was given away by an uncontrollable glimmer in his eye.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0048 }

“Mr. Pettifer, you are pleased that your wife has returned,” Nell exclaimed, pointing her finger toward him. “There is no need to act as though you are not, since it is obvious to me.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0049 }

A sheepish smile spread across Mr. Pettifer’s face as he relaxed.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0050 }

“Well . . . well . . . it is becoming familiar to me,” he acknowledged. “Seeing Emily was not something I regretted, I must admit. In a town of this nature, a man truly requires a degree of defense, since he cannot engage in a checkers match with a neighbor without people alleging he desires to wed the sister of that neighbor and publishing the claim in the newspaper.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0051 }

“If you had not acted as though you were single, no one would have believed you had gone to visit Isabella Pullen,” Nell remarked sternly.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0052 }

“I never claimed to be. Had anyone inquired whether I was a married man, I would have answered that I was. Everyone simply assumed it, however. I had no desire to discuss the subject . . . my feelings about it were still far too tender. Mrs. Agatha Sowerby would have been utterly delighted to learn that my wife had deserted me, would she not?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0053 }

“Yet certain individuals claim that you abandoned her.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0054 }

“Nell, she was the one who started it; it was her. I shall recount the entire tale to you, because I wish for you not to hold a poorer opinion of me than what I am due . . . or of Emily either. However, let us step out onto the porch. The sheer, frightening tidiness in this place somehow gives me a feeling of homesickness. It is likely that I will become accustomed to it in time, yet gazing at the yard brings me relief. Emily has not found the time to straighten it out as of now.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0055 }

The moment they had settled themselves comfortably on the veranda, Mr. Pettifer started to recount his tale of woe.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0056 }

“Prior to arriving at this place, Nell, my home was in Scottsford, New Brunswick. The housekeeping was handled by my sister, who satisfied me completely; her neatness was merely sensible, and she gave me my space while indulging me . . . according to Emily. However, her death occurred three years back. As her end approached, my future welfare caused her great anxiety, until she ultimately obtained my word that I would wed. Her counsel was for me to choose Emily Scott, owing to Emily possessing her own funds and being a model of domestic management. Says I, ‘Emily Scott wouldn’t look at me.’ My sister says, ‘You ask her and see;’ and simply to comfort her, I gave my word that I would . . . and I followed through. Whereupon Emily accepted my proposal. I was never more astonished in my life, Nell . . . a clever, attractive small woman such as her and a man of my advanced years. I assure you that initially I believed I was fortunate. Anyhow, our wedding took place, followed by a brief two-week honeymoon in St. John, after which we returned to our residence. Upon our arrival home at ten o’clock in the evening, I assure you on my honor, Nell, that within thirty minutes that woman had begun housecleaning. Ah, I realize you think my dwelling required it . . . your facial expression is highly telling, Nell; what you think appears upon it as clearly as type . . . yet it was not in such terrible shape. Granted, things had grown rather disarranged while I maintained a bachelor's residence, but prior to my marriage I had hired a woman to clean it thoroughly, and a great deal of painting and repairing had been completed. I assure you that if Emily were brought into a newly constructed white marble palace, she would start scrubbing the moment she could change into old clothes. Well, her housecleaning persisted until one o’clock that night, and by four o’clock she had risen to resume the task. And she continued in that manner . . . so far as I could tell, she never ceased. It was perpetual scouring, sweeping, and dusting, bar Sundays, though even then she eagerly anticipated the arrival of Monday to restart. Still, that was her chosen pastime, and I could have accepted it had she not bothered me. Yet she refused to refrain. She resolved to reform my character, but she had not acquired me at a sufficiently tender age. Permission to enter the dwelling was denied to me unless I swapped my boots for slippers right at the threshold. Upon my life, I dared not smoke a pipe unless I retreated to the barn. Furthermore, my grammar was insufficiently proper. In her younger days, Emily had served as a schoolteacher, a trait she had never outgrown. Additionally, she despised observing me eat using my knife. Well, that was the situation: ceaseless fault-finding and nagging. Yet I suppose, Nell, to remain impartial, I was also cross. I made no effort to better myself as I could have done . . . I merely became ill-tempered and unpleasant whenever she criticized me. I remarked to her one day that she had raised no objections to my grammar when I asked her to marry me. Saying that was hardly diplomatic. A woman would sooner pardon a husband for physically striking her than for implying she was overly delighted to secure him. At any rate, we continued squabbling in that fashion, which was hardly enjoyable, yet in time we might have adapted to one another had Nutmeg not interfered. Nutmeg proved to be the final point of contention that separated us. Emily disliked parrots and was unable to endure Nutmeg’s habit of using foul language. I felt an affection for the bird on account of my brother the sailor. As young children, my brother the sailor had been a favorite of mine, and he had dispatched Nutmeg to me during his final illness. I perceived no reason to become upset over the bird's cursing. Nothing is more repulsive to me than bad language from a person, but regarding a parrot, which merely echoes what it has overheard without comprehending it any more than I would comprehend Chinese, concessions should be granted. Emily, however, was incapable of viewing it from that perspective. Logic is lacking in women. She attempted to cure Nutmeg of cursing, yet she met with no greater triumph than when she attempted to stop me from uttering ‘I seen’ and ‘them things.’ It appeared that the harder she tried, the worse Nutmeg behaved, precisely like myself.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0057 }

“Well, matters continued in this manner, with both of us becoming increasingly irritated, until the final breaking point arrived. Emily asked our minister and his wife over for tea, along with a guest minister and his wife who were staying with them. I had given my word to stow Nutmeg away in a secure location where he could not be heard . . . Emily refused to touch his cage with a ten-foot pole . . . and I fully intended to do so, because I had no desire for the ministers to overhear anything disagreeable in my home. However, I forgot all about it . . . Emily was troubling me to such an extent regarding clean collars and proper grammar that it was hardly surprising . . . and that poor parrot never crossed my mind until we were seated for tea. Exactly while minister number one was right in the middle of offering the blessing, Nutmeg, who was perched on the veranda beyond the dining room window, began to shout. The gobbler had appeared in the yard, and seeing a gobbler constantly produced a bad reaction in Nutmeg. On that occasion, he outdid himself. You are welcome to smile, Nell, and I admit I have laughed about it a bit myself since then, but during the moment I experienced nearly as much embarrassment as Emily. I stepped outside and hauled Nutmeg off to the barn. I cannot claim that I found the meal pleasant. I gathered from Emily's expression that a storm was gathering for Nutmeg and James A. Once the guests departed, I headed toward the cow pasture, doing some deep reflecting along the way. I pitied Emily and somewhat believed I had not been as considerate of her as I could have been; furthermore, I questioned whether the ministers would suspect that Nutmeg had acquired his words from me. To make a long story short, I reached the conclusion that Nutmeg must be humanely done away with, and after I had driven the cows back home, I went inside to inform Emily of this. Yet Emily was nowhere to be found, and a letter was sitting on the table . . . exactly as it happens in fiction books. Emily had written that a choice must be made by me between her and Nutmeg; she had returned to her personal home, and she intended to remain there until I visited to inform her that I had disposed of the parrot.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0058 }

“My temper got the better of me, Nell, so I declared she could remain until judgment day if she was waiting for that, and I didn't back down. I gathered her things and had them forwarded to her. It caused a tremendous amount of rumor . . . Scottsford almost rivaled Brierley when it came to gossip . . . and all the townspeople took Emily's side. The whole affair left me perpetually ill-tempered and irritable, making me realize I needed to leave if I ever wanted tranquility. I made up my mind to relocate to the Island. I had visited during my childhood and enjoyed it; however, Emily had consistently claimed she refused to reside in a location where people were terrified to take evening strolls lest they tumble off the brim. Therefore, simply to be stubborn, I relocated to this side. And that covers the entire matter. I had not received any news concerning Emily until I returned from the rear pasture Saturday and discovered her washing the floor, though a initial proper meal I had tasted since her departure was already set upon the table. She instructed me to consume it before we discussed anything . . . which made me gather that Emily had absorbed a few truths regarding coexisting with a husband. Consequently, she has arrived and plans to remain . . . considering that Nutmeg has passed away and the Island proves somewhat larger than she imagined. That is Mrs. Sowerby alongside her at this moment. No, remain where you are, Nell. Stick around and become familiar with Emily. She developed quite a liking for you Saturday . . . inquiring about the identity of that attractive red-headed young lady residing next door.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0059 }

Nell was received with a radiant welcome by Mrs. Pettifer, who urged that she remain for tea.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0060 }

“James A. was just informing me about everything regarding you, as well as how good-natured you have been by baking cakes and other items for his benefit,” she remarked. “It is my desire to become familiar with every one of my new neighbors at the earliest opportunity. Mrs. Sowerby is a wonderful person, would you not agree? Extremely welcoming.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0061 }

As Nell returned to her house during the pleasant June evening, Mrs. Pettifer accompanied her through the meadows, where fireflies lit their starry lanterns.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0062 }

“I assume,” Mrs. Pettifer mentioned in confidence, “that James A. disclosed our history to you?”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0063 }

“Yes.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0064 }

“So there is no requirement for me to relate it, because James A. is an upright person and he’ll speak truthfully. He was by no means the only one at fault. Now I am able to recognize that. Before I had been home for even sixty minutes, I regretted my impatience, yet I refused to yield. At present, I realize my expectations for a man were excessive. Furthermore, taking offense at his poor grammar was truly silly of me. A husband's poor grammar is irrelevant provided he supplies well for the home and refrains from snooping in the pantry to check your weekly sugar consumption. My sense is that James A. and I will enjoy true happiness from now on. If only I were aware of ‘Observer’’s identity to express my thanks to him. My obligation to him for this favor is very great.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0065 }

Nell maintained her silence, leaving Mrs. Pettifer unaware that her thankfulness reached the person for whom it was intended. The wide-ranging repercussions of those senseless “notes” left Nell feeling somewhat confused. A husband and his wife had been reunited by them, and they had established a prophet's fame.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0066 }

Inside the kitchen at Grey Shutters, Mrs. Sowerby was located. To Thirza, she had been recounting the entire tale.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0067 }

“So, what is your opinion of Mrs. Pettifer?” she inquired of Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0068 }

“Extremely so. In my opinion, she’s a truly sweet small lady.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0069 }

“That is precisely what she is,” Mrs. Agatha stated emphatically, “and just as I was telling Thirza, it is my belief that we should all ignore Mr. Pettifer’s quirks on her account and endeavor to help her feel welcome here, indeed. Now, I have to return. Thomas will be missing me. Although I manage to leave the house a bit now that Eliza has arrived and he has appeared much improved over the last few days, I still dislike being gone from him for extended periods. I understand Hugh Carrow has stepped down from Pale Sands. I imagine he will be leaving for college this autumn.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0070 }

Mrs. Agatha cast a keen glance toward Nell, yet Nell was leaning down toward a drowsy Robin who was dozing on the couch, leaving her features impossible to decipher. She bore Robin off, pressing her rounded youthfulness of cheek against his bright ringlets. While they mounted the steps, Robin wrapped a weary arm around the neck of Nell, bestowing upon her an affectionate embrace and a tacky kiss.
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0071 }

“You’re extremely kind, Nell. On his slate today, Milty Gammon wrote a message and displayed it to Jennie Mott,
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0072 }

“‘Sugar is sweet, and you are too; vi’lets are blue, and roses red”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0073 }

and those words convey my sentiments toward you precisely, Nell.”
{: #nw-v02-c25-p0074 }
